evidence_set: Adults aged 21 to 70 who had used cannabis at least four times in the past month and had used, at least once, the strongest product that could be assigned (24% THC flower or 90% THC concentrate) with no adverse reaction; no other non-prescription drug in the past 60 days, no daily tobacco, light alcohol use. Within each form, participants were randomly assigned by random-number table to a labelled strength (flower 16% or 24%; concentrate 70% or 90%), bought it at a local dispensary that set allotments aside for the study, used it freely for 5 days, and on the fifth day the mobile laboratory came to their home: they gave the first measures there, used the product in their preferred way at home, and returned to the laboratory for the short-term post-use measures (mean 13.3 minutes away from it, range 3 to 47) and the 1-hour post-use measures. The form itself was each person's own choice.

Delayed recall and balance impairment were associated with short-term use even in regular consumers; people who used concentrates showed similar or lower subjective intoxication and short-term impairment than people who used lower-potency flower forms of cannabis; THC exposure was much higher in the concentrate group, prompting concern about long-term clinical and neurobehavioral implications. The Key Points say concentrates were associated with higher THC exposure and potentially greater risk. Long-term and clinical outcomes were not measured.
